  • If more water flows in through [MATH: C] than out through [MATH: C] (i.e., there is a net flow in through [MATH: C]), the flux is negative.

  • If the net flow through [MATH: C] is zero, the flux equals zero.

The outward-pointing unit normal vector tells us which direction is "out."

With that in mind, let's check each statement.

  • Statement I is false, while statement II is true. From the diagram below we see that [MATH: \mathbf F] acts perpendicular to [MATH: \mathbf n] at every point on [MATH: C.] Therefore, there is no net flow of [MATH: \mathbf F] through [MATH: C.]

    So, the flux of [MATH: \mathbf F] across [MATH: C] is zero, and we must have [MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.]

  • Statement III is false. When measuring flux through a closed curve, the orientation of the curve does not matter because the outward-pointing unit normal vector is the same at each point on [MATH: C] in either case.

    So, the flux of [MATH: \mathbf F] across [MATH: -C] is zero, and we must have [MATH: \oint\limits_{-C} \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s = 0.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let [MATH: \mathbf F] be a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb R^2] and [MATH: C] be a closed curve in the [MATH: xy]-plane. Imagine that [MATH: \mathbf F] represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water, and [MATH: C] is a curve that allows water to flow through it (like a fishing net).

Content:
The flux of [MATH: \mathbf F] across [MATH: \boldsymbol C] is a scalar number that tells us how much water is escaping the region bounded by [MATH: C.]

Content:
We have three possible scenarios:

Content:
- If more water flows out through [MATH: C] than in through [MATH: C] (i.e., there is a net flow out through [MATH: C]), the flux is positive.

[IMG: /graphics/df9e471bda3b6683a0dd149777d5e3f5]
- If more water flows in through [MATH: C] than out through [MATH: C] (i.e., there is a net flow in through [MATH: C]), the flux is negative.

[IMG: /graphics/e2d5922f878b632f2c86fea0a17b5c2a]
- If the net flow through [MATH: C] is zero, the flux equals zero.

The following vector field has zero flux across [MATH: C] because the amount of water flowing in through [MATH: C] equals the amount of water flowing out through [MATH: C.]

[IMG: /graphics/5ee9cd595acfac4ed2ff55d6f5e31338]

The following two vector fields also have a zero flux across [MATH: C] because the water flow is tangential to [MATH: C] at every point along [MATH: C.]

[IMG: /graphics/c42545d02cf09e50de1127972d6f188a]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Constructing an Integral Formula for the Flux

Content:
If [MATH: \mathbf{F}(x,y)] is a vector field on [MATH: \mathbb{R}^2] and [MATH: C] is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of [MATH: \mathbf F] across [MATH: C] is given by the line integral
[MATH: \oint\limits_C \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf{n} \: \textrm{d}s,]
where [MATH: \mathbf{n}] denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to [MATH: C.] The symbol [MATH: \oint\limits] means integration over the closed curve.

Content:
